question.text: The Black-Scholes option-pricing model values an option using which set of inputs?

answer.text: The credit rating of the issuer and the rating-agency outlook only
The price of the underlying asset, the exercise (strike) price, volatility of the underlying, the risk-free interest rate and the time to expiry
The book value of the underlying company and its current dividend yield only
The exchange's daily traded volume and the broker's commission rate

explanation.text: The Logic: The Black-Scholes model expresses the theoretical value of a European-style option as a function of (i) the spot price of the underlying asset, (ii) the strike or exercise price, (iii) the volatility of the underlying, (iv) the risk-free interest rate and (v) the time remaining until expiry. These inputs feed into the standard Black-Scholes formula and are the variables a Category III AIF manager would focus on when pricing or risk-managing an options book. The Trap: Credit ratings and rating outlooks are inputs for assessing debt instruments, not for pricing standard equity options. Book value and dividend yield alone do not capture volatility, time decay or interest-rate effects that drive option prices. Exchange volume and broker commissions are transaction-cost or liquidity considerations rather than inputs to the theoretical option-price model. Note: The cited workbook chapter discusses the Black-Scholes model and its standard inputs (underlying price, exercise price, volatility, interest rates and time to expiry). The earlier formulation of this question tested option-Greek "gamma" as the sensitivity of delta to underlying-price changes, which is not present in the cited chapter. The current framing is aligned with the workbook's coverage and general options-pricing knowledge.
